tldr: By integrating minimal geometric guiding structures (SIE, IGT, and HOP) into reinforcement learning, the authors solved the long-standing challenge of whole-body humanoid transport tasks characterized by high dimensionality, rich contact, and long horizons. They demonstrated the first fully autonomous, unassisted transfer of a medical training mannequin from a bed to a wheelchair using a real humanoid robot.
hero_caption: A sequence of real-robot motions where the humanoid robot AIREC lifts a medical training mannequin (155 cm, 15 kg) lying on a bed and transfers it to a wheelchair. Unlike conventional assistive robots that require human help during the process, this transfer is completed fully autonomously by replaying a policy learned in simulation.
overview:
Whole-body object transport using humanoid robots has long been an open problem in robotics. Conventional reinforcement learning (RL) exploration breaks down because three severe difficulties hit all at once: a high-dimensional space combining the robot's own 35 degrees of freedom with the object's degrees of freedom, complex discontinuous contacts during hugging/lifting, and a long-horizon, non-periodic task that sequentially chains distinct skills like grasping, carrying, and placing.

To address this, the authors propose three geometric structures that cleverly guide exploration without stripping away the policy's degrees of freedom. First, Sparse Interaction Edges (SIE) align observations and rewards along edges connecting keypoints on the robot and the object, promoting whole-body hugging. Second, Interaction Gated Transport (IGT) gates the transport reward based on these edge distances, preventing degenerate behaviors like throwing and maintaining tight, close-contact carrying. Finally, Hinted Object Path (HOP) supplies a rough reference trajectory for the object alone to bypass obstacles, preventing the policy from getting stuck in local minima.

Experiments evaluated tasks ranging from rigid sphere transport to transferring a human from a bed to a wheelchair. Using a single consumer GPU (RTX 5090), tasks were mastered in under an hour of training. Furthermore, policies learned in simulation were deployed to the real dual-arm mobile humanoid AIREC, successfully transferring a medical mannequin from a bed to a wheelchair without human intervention. The approach also showed remarkable robustness to substantial variations in body size, weight, and external disturbances.
contributions: Integrated observations and rewards using edges connecting keypoints between the robot and object (SIE), eliminating blind search in joint space to achieve whole-body coordinated cradling.
Introduced a gating mechanism (IGT) that softly modulates transport rewards based on SIE distances, curbing degenerative failures such as throwing the object during long-horizon transport.

Provided hints only for the object's rough spatial path rather than robot joint trajectories (HOP), avoiding contact discontinuities with obstacles while preserving the policy's freedom to discover strategies.
Achieved the first fully autonomous whole-body mannequin transfer from a bed to a wheelchair on a physical humanoid without any human assistance.

sections.heading: Why is humanoid patient transfer the ultimate frontier for reinforcement learning?
sections.summary: While reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable results in drone racing and quadruped parkour, whole-body humanoid manipulation remains a major hurdle. The root cause is a trilemma of high dimensionality, discontinuous contact, and long, non-periodic horizons. This paper tackles bed-to-wheelchair transfer—one of the most pressing needs in caregiving—to solve it.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful framework capable of discovering unique ways to use a body in simulation that differ from human motions. In whole-body humanoid manipulation, however, most prior successes have relied on human motion imitation or pre-planned trajectories. Pure RL on its own has largely remained confined to handovers of small rigid objects or simple box carrying.

The authors point out that this wall stems from three intertwined bottlenecks (a trilemma):
- High dimensionality from robot-object coupling: In addition to the robot's own 35 degrees of freedom (DoF), the 15 DoF of the human model must be controlled and considered simultaneously, causing the exploration space to explode.
- Discontinuous optimization landscape due to contact-rich environments: Isotropic Gaussian exploration in joint space quickly leads to collisions or rigid constraints in narrow gaps between the bed and human body, destroying smooth gradients.
- Long, non-periodic task horizons: Unlike periodic motions such as locomotion, the robot must sequentially execute completely distinct skills—lifting, carrying, and carefully seating—making credit assignment (evaluating which actions led to success) extraordinarily difficult.

Bed-to-wheelchair transfer is not only immensely valuable in the real world to alleviate caregiver back pain and severe labor shortages; it serves as the ultimate benchmark embodying all three challenges. Rather than imposing rigid constraints that rob the policy of flexibility, the authors tackled this challenge by providing minimal task structures that serve as signposts for exploration.

captions.F2: Comparison of learning curves (top) and learned strategies (bottom) between the proposed method and baseline RL. Baselines converge to abnormal solutions such as throwing the human or lifting only by one leg or the head, whereas the proposed method stably acquires a natural whole-body cradling transport strategy across all five random seeds.

sections.heading: From balls to humans: How the proposed method unlocks breakthrough transport performance
sections.summary: Evaluated across rigid sphere transport and two human transfer setups (near and far with an obstacle), the proposed method achieved stable whole-body transport across all seeds, whereas baselines failed completely. It proved robust to body variations and disturbances, and was verified on a real robot transferring a mannequin.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted in Isaac Lab using AIREC, a mobile humanoid robot with 35 degrees of freedom. Three evaluation tasks were studied: depositing a rigid sphere into a box (Ball), transferring from a bed to a nearby wheelchair (Human (near)), and transferring around an obstacle over a longer distance (Human (far)).

### Training Efficiency and Baseline Comparisons
The computational cost of the proposed method is remarkably light. On a single RTX 5090 GPU, it reaches practical performance in about 30 minutes for the Ball environment and about 60 minutes for the Human environments with heavy contact computations. Conversely, baseline RL configured with standard joint-angle observations and end-effector-to-goal distance rewards simply rolled the ball with one hand without lifting it, and in the Human environments degenerated into throwing the human into the air or grabbing only the head, failing the far transfer entirely.

### Effects of the Three Core Components
Ablation experiments clearly isolated the role of each building block:
- Introducing SIE (edge structures): By considering keypoints on forearms and chest rather than just hands, the strategy shifted dramatically from one-handed pushing to whole-body two-arm cradling.
- Introducing IGT (gating mechanism): By cutting off transport rewards when the robot and object separated, it eliminated cheating behaviors like throwing the object after lifting, yielding consistent behavior that maintained close-contact carrying.
- Introducing HOP (hinted trajectories): By providing coarse trajectory hints that clear obstacles and the wheelchair frame, the policy escaped local optima of ramming directly into obstacle walls and discovered safe detour paths.

### Surprising Generalization and Disturbance Adaptation
Most notably, the policy adapted without any additional training. A single policy successfully transferred humans with broad morphological differences ranging from 11 to 33 kg in weight and 115 to 180 cm in height. Moreover, when trained under environments with large random external forces of 300 to 500 N applied to the object, the robot spontaneously learned a firmer cradling strategy—wrapping its arms deeply and pulling the object tightly against its chest—even though no such instruction was given in the reward.

### Real-Robot Mannequin Transfer with AIREC
When trajectories from the learned policy were replayed open-loop on the real AIREC robot, it successfully lifted an articulated medical mannequin (155 cm, 15 kg) from a bed, turned 90 degrees, and accurately seated it in a wheelchair. This succeeded both when the wheelchair was placed near the head of the bed and near the foot, marking the first time a humanoid has achieved mannequin transfer without human assistance.

The policy follows the hint 100% initially, but later departs appropriately as its own optimization takes over.

(b) When random external force disturbances are applied to the object, the robot spontaneously learns a firmer grasping strategy, pulling the human deep into its chest.

sections.heading: Providing hints instead of constraints: Design philosophy and hurdles for real-world deployment
sections.summary: The core essence of the proposed method is that it does not bind the robot with rigid rules, but instead achieves dramatic exploration guidance using hints that account for just 5–10% of total rewards. The authors discuss the value of general-purpose humanoids in caregiving while outlining remaining motor torque and safety challenges for real humans.
sections.details:
Why can such simple guidance solve an otherwise intractable problem? This is the paper's key insight. The guiding rewards from SIE, IGT, and HOP account for only 5 to 10% of the total return across an episode. In other words, these structures are not absolute commands; they act as gentle nudges pushing exploration into promising regions. In fact, while the robot tracks the hint trajectory early in training, it autonomously reshapes it later on into motions that are more natural and efficient for its own body.

Regarding the rationale for using general-purpose humanoids rather than dedicated patient lifts, the authors point to the versatility of handling diverse care tasks with a single hardware platform and the extensibility to accompany humans beyond the bedside—across uneven ground or into public transit. While earlier Japanese nursing-care robots (such as RI-MAN and RIBA) were semi-autonomous systems requiring human caregivers to lift legs or assist, the RL approach here opens the door to complete autonomy.

At the same time, clear barriers remain before moving from mannequins to real living humans:
- Engineering limits on motor torque: Holding a 50 kg human requires roughly 375 Nm of torque at the shoulder joints, but AIREC's current rating is limited to 220 Nm.
- Safety guarantees against catastrophic failure: Neural network policies lack guarantees against unexpected actions. Integrating contact force limiters and whole-body tactile sensing for real-time slip and pinch detection will be essential going forward.

captions.F6: Stepwise ablation results in the Ball environment. Starting from the baseline, sequentially enabling SIE (whole-body cradling), IGT (anti-throwing and holding), and HOP (detour path over the box edge) clearly shows how the motion is refined to achieve task success.

sections.heading: Three structured approaches to compress exploration and analytical bandwidth computation (ABC)
sections.summary: The proposed framework consists of SIE (Sparse Interaction Edges), IGT (Interaction Gated Transport), HOP (Hinted Object Path), and ABC (Analytical Bandwidth Computation) to analytically determine reward scales. It works solely by augmenting observations and rewards, requiring no changes to standard RL algorithms like PPO.
sections.details:
Because every component of this method acts exclusively on the observation space and reward function of the Markov Decision Process (MDP), it can be combined with any standard reinforcement learning algorithm.

### 1. Sparse Interaction Edges (SIE)
Conventional RL typically observes only robot joint angles and end-effector positions, which severely hampers exploration for whole-body manipulation. SIE places sparse keypoints on both the robot (8 points including mobile base, chest, upper arms, forearms, and hands) and the object (5 points in the human case: shoulders, waist, and thighs), defining 3D edge vectors connecting them. Rewarding the shortening of these edge lengths perfectly aligns observation features with optimization gradients, dramatically speeding up convergence toward whole-body contact configurations.

### 2. Interaction Gated Transport (IGT)
Standard transport rewards measure only the distance between the object and the target, which incentivizes the robot to exploit rewards by throwing the object. IGT evaluates whether the robot-object SIE edge lengths are within a threshold (0.3 m in Human environments) using a sigmoid function, applying it as a soft multiplicative gate to the transport reward. Consequently, transport rewards are paid only while the object is held close to the body, naturally enforcing secure, close-contact carrying.

### 3. Hinted Object Path (HOP)
When obstacles exist, rewarding only target proximity directs the steepest descent straight into obstacle walls, trapping the policy in local minima. HOP provides a coarse 4th-order Bézier curve from initial to target positions as a hint trajectory for the object's keypoints. The agent receives rewards based on progress along path waypoints and tracking error. Crucially, HOP specifies only the spatial route the object should traverse, not robot joint trajectories; how the robot coordinates its body to realize that route remains entirely free.

### 4. Analytical Bandwidth Computation (ABC)
In hyperbolic tangent transformations used to normalize distances in reward terms, tuning the bandwidth parameter $k$ traditionally requires tedious trial and error. ABC derives an analytical formula to uniquely determine $k$ based on the geometric initial condition that the reward equals $r_0 = 0.05$ at the initial distance $\delta$. This completely removes the need for hyperparameter tuning via trial and error.

captions.F3: Conceptual diagram of the three proposed geometric guidance methods. 1. Shortening keypoint distances via SIE, 2. Proximity-dependent transport reward gating via sigmoid-based IGT, and 3. Coarse HOP reference trajectories guiding the object to the goal while bypassing local minima. All three elements work together seamlessly.

sections.heading: Appendix: Overcoming Sim-to-Real hurdles and the limits of imitation learning
sections.summary: Zero-shot transfer from simulation to the real AIREC robot overcame discrepancies with impedance controllers, strict anti-tipping protections (ZMP monitoring), and excessive contact forces on the wheelchair. The authors also document experiments showing that collecting human demonstrations via teleoperation was physically impractical.
sections.details:
In transferring policies trained in simulation (Isaac Lab, 120 Hz physics, 30 Hz control) to the real hardware, the authors addressed several critical Sim-to-Real gaps.

### Five Challenges in Hardware Deployment and Solutions
- Controller dynamics mismatch: While the simulator assumed an ideal PD control law, the physical robot ran on unmodeled impedance controllers, causing torque commands to diverge at higher speeds. This was resolved by replaying motions at one-third control frequency (10 Hz) during real-world execution to stabilize behavior.
- Anti-tipping safety mechanism (ZMP monitoring): The physical robot features a safety mechanism that triggers an immediate emergency stop if the Zero Moment Point (ZMP) exits a $12\times 12\text{ cm}^2$ support base. Imposing a severe penalty (-1000) for ZMP excursions and providing ZMP information in observations kept the robot in stable postures.
- Contact forces with the wheelchair: In simulation, the wheelchair was fixed to the floor, allowing the policy to cheat by bracing against the chair to wedge itself in. Because this would topple the real wheelchair, the wheelchair's collision mesh was expanded to prevent physical contact.
- Real-world geometric calibration: Mannequin link dimensions were accurately measured and mirrored in simulation, and wrists and knees were loosely bound to suppress joint flailing during physical trials.
- Torque and position error limits: Seating requires delicate lowering motions that often triggered hard stops from joint torque limits; workspace height adjustments (such as elevating wheelchairs) were noted as effective for complete success.

### Failure of Teleoperation (Imitation Learning)
Addressing why RL was necessary in the first place, the authors report attempts to collect demonstrations via master-slave robot puppets. When trying to lift the 15 kg mannequin via teleoperation, the mannequin slid down faster than human operator reflexes could compensate, preventing even skilled operators from achieving stable lifts. This outcome underscores that for handling heavy, contact-rich objects, RL's ability to learn high-output, reflexive closed-loop control is fundamentally superior to imitating human demonstrations.

captions.F8: Attempts and limitations of imitation learning. Top: human demonstration of caregiving motion. Bottom: teleoperation attempt using a robot puppet. Operator feedback could not keep pace with the mannequin sliding under its own weight, causing teleoperated data collection itself to fail.

takeaways: Aligning observations and rewards using edges between robot and object keypoints (SIE), rather than exploring blindly in joint space, is extraordinarily effective for learning whole-body coordination.
In long-horizon transport tasks, gating transport rewards on robot-object proximity (IGT) rather than raw target distance drastically suppresses degenerate behaviors like throwing.
Providing coarse spatial paths only for the object (HOP) without constraining robot joint trajectories harmonizes obstacle avoidance with the free discovery of viable strategies.

Because heavy, contact-rich cradling involves slipping speeds that exceed human reaction times, acquiring reflexive closed-loop control through reinforcement learning offers a clear edge over imitation learning.
limitations: Real-robot validation was limited to open-loop trajectory replay and has not yet demonstrated closed-loop real-time control or disturbance adaptation using sensor feedback.
The current shoulder torque of AIREC (220 Nm) lacks the physical capacity required to lift the average weight of an adult human (roughly 50 kg or more).
The approach assumes accurate external perception of object keypoint locations and has yet to integrate whole-body tactile sensing for contact state estimation or physical safety guards.
